summaries.example: Imagine you say, “Kindness is a quality.” A reist might try to restate this as “Some people are kind.” The second sentence talks about particular people instead of treating “kindness” as a separate thing. Reists think this can make our words clearer.
summaries.summary: Reism is a philosophical idea about what exists. It says that only things exist, but philosophers who defend it do not always agree about what counts as a thing. Franz Brentano included bodies and souls. Tadeusz Kotarbiński gave a stronger version in which every thing is a material body. Reism also makes a suggestion about language: we should prefer names for concrete individuals and be careful with abstract words such as “property” or “relation.” An abstract sentence may be acceptable if it can be restated using names for things. Reists thought this could stop people from arguing about things that exist only in thought. The source also explains that reism faces hard problems, especially when we try to use it to explain mathematics, language, minds, society, or art.
key_ideas: Reism says that only things exist.
Some reists try to replace abstract words with words for particular things.
Brentano allowed both bodies and souls as things.
Kotarbiński’s version said that every thing is a material body.
Reists hoped to prevent confusing arguments about imaginary abstract objects.
summaries.why_it_matters: Reism asks us to look closely at the words we use. Sometimes a word can make an idea sound like a separate object. Reists believe that replacing such words with clearer sentences about things may prevent mistakes. The view also shows that philosophers can agree on a general idea while disagreeing about whether souls, minds, or only bodies belong in the world.

important_terms.definition: The view that only things, especially individual concrete things, exist.
A real, individual thing that we can encounter, such as a person or a body.
A word that seems to name an idea or quality rather than a concrete thing.
Treating an idea as if it were a real thing when it may not be one.

questions_to_think_about: Can every sentence about an idea be changed into a sentence about particular things?
Are words such as “redness” useful even if they do not name separate things?
Would a world containing only physical bodies leave anything important out?

summaries.example: Consider the sentence, “Wisdom is a property of some people.” A reist can treat “wisdom” and “property” as apparent names rather than genuine names of objects. Kotarbiński would prefer the reistic version, “Some people are wise,” because it speaks about individuals and their actions or characteristics without naming abstract objects. The point is not merely stylistic: the rewrite is meant to avoid commitment to properties as entities.
summaries.summary: Reism is the doctrine that only things exist, but its philosophical force depends on how “thing” and “exist” are interpreted. A broad reistic thesis says that only particulars or concreta exist; this connects reism with nominalism. Brentano’s later ontology identifies being with real things and rejects entities that exist only in thought, such as universals, relations, possibilities, and states of affairs. He distinguishes bodies, which are extended in space and time, from souls, which are extended only in time. His analysis of abstract sentences aims to show how they can be understood without naming abstract objects. Kotarbiński develops a more systematic and materialist version. His ontological reism says that every object is a thing and that no object is a property, relation, or state of affairs. Pansomatism then defines every thing as a material body. His semantic reism divides names into genuine names and onomatoids. Sentences containing onomatoids are meaningful only when they can be translated into sentences containing genuine names and logical constants. This strategy is designed to block hypostatization, especially in philosophical debates. The entry nevertheless emphasizes that reism has only partial success. Its principles themselves can seem to use the abstract terms they reject, and its application to mathematics, semantics, psychology, social rules, and works of art remains difficult. The source therefore presents later reism more as a research program than as a complete theory.
key_ideas: The broad thesis shared by several forms of reism is that only particulars or concreta exist.
Brentano’s reism rejects entia rationis, including relations, universals, possibilities, and states of affairs, as independently existing objects.
Kotarbiński formulates reism through the claims that every object is a thing and that no object is a state of affairs, relation, or property.
Kotarbiński’s pansomatism identifies things with material bodies, making his version monistic and materialist, unlike Brentano’s body-and-soul dualism.
Semantic reism distinguishes genuine names from apparent names and permits abstract sentences only when they have reistic translations.
The entry presents reism as facing substantial difficulties in mathematics, logic, semantics, psychology, sociology, and the humanities.
summaries.why_it_matters: Reism connects metaphysics with the philosophy of language. It asks whether the grammar of a sentence encourages us to believe in entities that are not really there. Its differences between Brentano and Kotarbiński also show that a shared formal principle—only particulars exist—can receive different metaphysical interpretations. At the same time, the difficulties of applying reism across many fields illustrate how demanding it is to build a completely concrete language and ontology.

important_terms.definition: An ontology claiming that things are the only ontological category, though reists disagree about which things qualify.
The study of what kinds of entities exist and how they are categorized.
A concrete individual, rather than a universal, relation, property, or other abstract entity.
A theory about which expressions genuinely name objects and how apparently abstract sentences can be translated.
The claim that all objects are material, spatially extended, and resistant bodies.
An expression that appears to name an abstract object but does not genuinely refer to one within reism.
A theory of parts and wholes, proposed by Kotarbiński as a possible aid for reistic analysis.
The mistake of treating an apparent abstract object as though it really existed.

questions_to_think_about: Does showing that an abstract sentence can be paraphrased in terms of individuals prove that abstract objects do not exist?
Is Brentano’s argument from the directedness of thought an argument for reism specifically, or only for a one-category ontology?
Can a theory of parts and wholes replace the explanatory work usually done by sets?
If a sentence contains an apparent name but has no reistic translation, should it be called false, meaningless, or something else?
Can natural language be fully understood without abstract nouns?

summaries.example: Suppose a student says, “Fairness is a rule that exists in the classroom.” A reist might ask what this sentence means in terms of actual people, actions, or written instructions. It could perhaps become, “The teacher treats students by the same rule,” or “The classroom rules tell students to take turns.” If no such clearer restatement is possible, a strict semantic reist may say the original sentence is not meaningful in the required way.
summaries.summary: Reism is the view that only things exist. This sounds simple, but the source explains that reists disagree about what counts as a thing. Franz Brentano’s later reism rejects objects that exist only in thought, including universals, relations, possibilities, and states of affairs. He accepts two kinds of things: bodies and souls. Tadeusz Kotarbiński develops a different version. He says that every object is a thing and that no object is a property, relation, or state of affairs. His idea of pansomatism adds that every thing is a material body, so his reism is a form of materialism. Reism also concerns language. Kotarbiński distinguishes genuine names, which refer to things, from onomatoids, which appear to name abstract objects. A sentence with an onomatoid may be meaningful if it can be translated into a sentence using genuine names. For instance, a statement about “wisdom” can be rewritten as a statement about people who are wise. Reists think this method prevents hypostatization: treating abstract ways of speaking as evidence for abstract objects. The entry also describes objections and limits. Some reistic claims seem to contain the very abstract terms that reism rejects. It is also difficult to give reistic accounts of mathematics, meaning, psychology, social rules, and works of art. For this reason, Kotarbiński eventually treated reism more as a program for improving thought and language than as a finished description of everything that exists.
key_ideas: Reism reduces the many kinds of entities proposed by some philosophers to one category: things.
Brentano and Kotarbiński both reject abstract objects, but Brentano accepts souls while Kotarbiński identifies things with material bodies.
Kotarbiński gives reism two sides: an ontological claim about objects and a semantic theory about names.
A sentence using an apparent name can still be acceptable if it can be translated into a sentence about genuine names for things.
Reists argue that abstract language can lead philosophers into unnecessary disputes.
The entry reports serious challenges when reism is applied to mathematics, logic, mental life, society, and art.
summaries.why_it_matters: Reism matters because it combines a theory of reality with a discipline for speaking carefully. It challenges us to ask whether a sentence really needs to refer to properties, relations, or other abstract entities. Comparing Brentano’s and Kotarbiński’s versions also teaches an important philosophical lesson: people may share a general principle while disagreeing about its consequences. The problems facing reism show why a simple rule about “things” may be hard to apply to every area of knowledge.

important_terms.definition: The philosophical position that only things exist; different reists disagree about what belongs among things.
A real individual object, such as a person or physical body, rather than a general idea.
A philosophical account of what exists and what kinds of entities there are.
The part of reism concerned with how names and sentences refer, or appear to refer, to objects.
Kotarbiński’s view that every object is a material, extended, resistant body.
A word that looks like a name for an abstract object, even though reism denies that such an object exists.
Mistaking a useful way of speaking for proof that an abstract object is real.

questions_to_think_about: Is “fairness” only a convenient word for fair actions, or could it name something real?
Why might replacing abstract nouns with sentences about people make an argument clearer?
Could a theory that accepts only bodies explain thoughts and social rules?
Does the fact that children learn concrete words before abstract nouns support reism, or only describe language development?
What might be lost if philosophy avoided every abstract term?
